# The Last Dial Tone

My job is to listen to things disappear.

There is an archive—I'm not permitted to say where—whose entire purpose is to record sounds that are going extinct. Not music, not famous speeches, not birdsong, though we keep those too. We collect the accidental sounds. The ones no one ever meant to make. The sounds that were nobody's intention and everybody's atmosphere.

Consider the dial tone. A steady drone, 350 hertz braided with 440, pouring into millions of kitchens for half a century. Nobody loved it. Nobody chose it. And yet when the last analog exchanges were decommissioned, letters arrived at telephone companies from people who said they missed it the way you'd miss a wall you used to lean against.

That is the kind of thing we keep.

We have the clatter of a Linotype machine, recorded in 1987 in the basement of a newspaper that no longer exists. We have the pneumatic sigh of subway doors from four different cities. Chalk on slate—dozens of samples, because every classroom struck the board differently, the way every pianist strikes middle C differently. Film projectors. Cash registers with real bells. Rotary dials returning home, that long ratcheted exhale. The thunk of a payphone receiver hung up in anger, and again, separately, in relief. The whir of a cassette rewinding, which an entire generation heard as the sound of anticipation itself. You cannot explain to a child that waiting used to have a noise.

People assume we are nostalgic. We are not, exactly. Nostalgia wants to return. We know there is no return. What we do is closer to habitat preservation. These sounds were rooms. People lived inside them. My colleague says a childhood is largely a set of noises, and I believe her. Ask anyone over fifty to describe feeling safe and see how long it takes them to mention a sound—the screen door, the neighbor's lawnmower, a baseball game murmuring on a radio in another room, unintelligible and therefore perfect.

Here is what I've learned in nineteen years: the rarest sounds are not the obsolete machines. Machines leave documentation. Somewhere there is always a working model, an enthusiast, a video shot in somebody's garage. No—the rarest sounds are human ones, made casually, by people who didn't know they were worth keeping. The specific way your grandmother said your name when you were in trouble. The two-note whistle my father used to call the dog, so characteristic that neighbors recognized it through their own closed windows.

I never recorded my father. I was seventeen and he was a noise I lived inside, and you do not archive the air.

He died when I was twenty-four. For years afterward I tried to rebuild that whistle in my head, and I could get the shape of it—the rising interval, the little scoop at the end—but never the pitch. Do you understand what that means? I remembered everything about the sound except the sound. Memory kept the notation and lost the music. Some nights I stood in my kitchen trying to produce it, and what came out was close enough to break me open and not close enough to help.

So yes, I work here. Call it penance if you want to be dramatic. I prefer to think of it as standing guard.

Our collection holds ninety thousand items. The oldest is a wax cylinder from 1890: a man imitating a turkey. The most requested is rain on a tin roof. But the item our director calls the crown jewel cost eleven cents to mail—it arrived in a padded envelope with no note. A cassette labeled, in ballpoint, *Sunday*. On it: forty minutes of a family eating breakfast. Plates. A chair scraping. Someone asking someone else to pass the jam. A baby beating a spoon in strict rhythm, then losing interest. A television talking to itself in the next room. Nothing happens for forty minutes. It is the greatest thing we own.

I listened to it the week it arrived and understood my whole profession at once. Every archive of cathedrals and presidents is, underneath, an attempt to get back to this tape. To the jam. To the spoon.

Lately I've started a side project, unofficial, off the books. When school groups visit, I tell the children to go home and do one thing: press record on whatever device they own, set it on the kitchen counter, and leave the room. Come back in an hour. Don't perform. Don't narrate. Just let the house talk.

Most of them never do it. Kids don't. But some do, and years later—this has happened three times now—a young adult writes to us, or appears in person, holding a phone or a battered drive, sometimes crying, sometimes laughing, asking whether we can take it. Their own voice has changed. Someone on the recording has died. The kitchen itself is gone—sold, painted, demolished—and here it all still is: the refrigerator's hum, the dog's tags, a mother calling up the stairs, bored, fond, entirely unaware.

We always say yes. It doesn't matter what's on it. Especially it doesn't matter what's on it.

I'll tell you what I tell them, and now I suppose I'm telling you. Tonight, or tomorrow, put a recorder near the people you love and walk away. Don't announce it. Don't make it an occasion. An occasion changes the acoustics of a life. Just capture an hour of the ordinary static of your household—the dishes, the complaints, the half-listened-to news, footsteps crossing the room above you.

Nothing will happen on that recording.

That's how you'll know it's priceless.
